title: LSM trees, SSTables and Bloom filters
goal: By the end, you can explain how an LSM tree turns many scattered writes into one long write, follow a write, a flush, a read and a merge through memory and sorted files, size a Bloom filter, and say when an LSM tree beats a B+tree and when it loses.
opening:
Picture the payments company adding a fraud check. Every tap of every card, in every shop, now saves a small record of a few dozen bytes. Each record gets a random id, so card readers everywhere can make ids at once without picking the same one. The table already holds a million records. The next 10,000 carry 240 KB of data, and the database writes 26 MB to its log alone to store them.

It's easy to blame the disk, or to think an id is an id. Random ids are the standard advice, and each insert is one small row, so it looks cheap.

In B+trees, we built a tree that finds any key in a few page reads. In this lesson, we'll count what a random key costs that tree, then build a store that never changes a file once it's written. We'll follow a read through its files, skip most of them with 10 bits per key, and weigh both designs with Facebook's numbers. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A store keeps its data in 6 sorted files on disk that never change once written, plus a sorted list in memory for the newest writes. You look up a key that is in none of them. How many of the 6 files does the lookup usually read from disk?
options: All 6, because the key could be in any of them
1, because the newest file has an entry for every key
About 3, because it halves the files at each step, like a binary search
Usually none: a small filter in memory for each file rules most of them out
warmup.why: Each file has a Bloom filter in memory, a few bits per key that can say "this key is definitely not here". For a key that was never added, a filter of 10 bits per key says "maybe" only about 1% of the time, so the lookup almost never touches the disk. Without filters, it would read a block from all 6 files. The files are separate sorted piles, so there's no binary search across them, and the newest file only holds the newest writes.

sections.h: Random keys make a B+tree rewrite a page for every insert
sections.body:
Let's measure the opening's problem. The tree from B+trees changes data in place. To insert a key, PostgreSQL, a free database program, finds the leaf where the key belongs: a page on the tree's bottom level. It changes that 8 KB page in memory, and later writes the whole page back to disk. When keys arrive in order, they all land on the rightmost leaf, and one page takes hundreds of inserts before it's written. When keys are random, every insert lands on a different leaf.

The keys here are UUIDs: 16-byte ids that any computer can make on its own with almost no chance of a clash. PostgreSQL's `gen_random_uuid()` makes random ones, and `uuidv7()` makes ones that start with the time, so each is bigger than the last.

In the Try it, each kind fills a table of a million rows. Then 10,000 more time-ordered rows dirty 105 pages: they change 105 pages in memory that must later be written back. And they write 1.5 MB to the write-ahead log, the file where PostgreSQL notes every change before it makes it. The same number of random rows dirty 4,278 pages and write 26.5 MB to the log. Most of that is whole pages. After a checkpoint, a moment when PostgreSQL has saved every page to disk, the first change to each page copies the entire page into the log. Write-ahead logging and crash recovery explains why.

The new rows hold 24 bytes of data each, 240 KB in all. So the store writes over 100 bytes for every byte it keeps: a write amplification above 100. And the 4,278 dirty pages still have to reach the disk later: about 33 MB more, in scattered 8 KB pieces.

Version 1 is the store from Bytes, pages and durability: a log-structured store. It appends every write to the end of one file. Every write is sequential, right after the one before, which is the cheapest thing a disk does. But the file has no order. Reads need a map of every key in memory, and ranges are out.

Version 2 keeps the cheap writes and gets the order back by sorting in memory first. A clerk with a pile of forms knows the trick. Filing each form in its drawer means a walk across the room per form. So she keeps a tray on her desk in order, and when it's full, she binds it into a booklet and shelves it, newest in front.

The tray is the **memtable**: a sorted map in memory that takes every new write. It's a `TreeMap` in the lab and a skip list, another sorted structure, in RocksDB, a free storage library from Facebook that many databases build on. Writing to the memtable costs no disk work. When it reaches a size limit, 64 MB by default in RocksDB, the whole memtable goes to disk in key order as one file, the booklet. Google's 2006 paper on Bigtable, its own storage system, named it a sorted string table, or **SSTable**. One sequential write of 64 MB replaces thousands of scattered page writes.

An SSTable never changes after it's written. An update puts a newer version of the key into the memtable, and it later lands in a newer SSTable. A delete writes a **tombstone**, a marker that says "this key is deleted". So the disk holds a growing stack of files, newest on top, and older files may still hold old versions of a key.

That design is the **log-structured merge tree**, or LSM tree, described by Patrick O'Neil and three colleagues in 1996. RocksDB is one. So are Cassandra and ScyllaDB, databases that spread data over many computers, and Pebble, which stores the data of the database CockroachDB. The figure is the picture for this lesson. Beside the memtable sits a write-ahead log, because the memtable lives in memory and a crash would wipe it. Next, we'll open an SSTable and follow a read down the stack.

try.title: Count what random keys cost a B+tree
steps: From the `labs` folder, start PostgreSQL with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`. Docker runs programs in sealed boxes called containers. Then open psql, PostgreSQL's window for typing SQL commands, with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz`.

Create two tables with a UUID primary key (the column that names each row, with a B-tree index on it) and a million rows each: one filled with time-ordered `uuidv7()` ids, one with random `gen_random_uuid()` ids. The inserts take several seconds.

`CHECKPOINT` makes PostgreSQL save every changed page now, so both tests start alike. After it, insert 10,000 more rows into each table. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, WAL ...)` runs the insert and reports its `Buffers` and `WAL` lines. Predict which insert writes more to the log, and by how much.
Stop PostgreSQL before the next Try it, which needs the memory for Cassandra: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down -v`.

sections.h: Reading a stack of sorted files, newest first
sections.body:
Inside, an SSTable is records in key order. Each record is a key length, the key, a value length and the value, as in the lab. The records are grouped into blocks: 4 KB by default in RocksDB, 16 records in the lab. Because the file is sorted, it doesn't need an index entry for every key. A **sparse index** holds only the first key of each block and where that block starts in the file.

To find `auth:00500`, search the sparse index for the last block whose first key isn't above it, read that one block, and scan it. In the lab, 1,000 records need 63 index entries, and a lookup costs exactly one read. The index is small, so the database keeps it in memory. RocksDB loads it, with the Bloom filter of the next section, when it opens a file.

Now the harder question: which file holds the key? A key can be in the memtable and in any number of SSTables, and only the newest version is right. So a read looks in the memtable first, then in the SSTables from newest to oldest, and stops at the first one that knows the key. If that first hit is a tombstone, the answer is "not found", and the older files must not be asked. The clerk does the same: tray first, then booklets from the front of the shelf. The stepper runs this with two files and one tombstone.

Cassandra, in the Try it, is an LSM tree you can watch at work, and two details differ from the lab. Cassandra stores each column of a row as a separate cell with its own timestamp. So an SSTable may hold only some columns of a row, and a read may need several files to rebuild one row: the trace for id 7 merges two. And Cassandra sorts each file by a hash of the key, a scrambled number worked out from it, so ids 7 and 8 aren't neighbours on disk.

The cost shows up for keys that aren't in the newest files. A key that only the oldest of 20 SSTables holds costs 19 useless block reads first, and a key that exists nowhere costs 20. The number of disk reads per lookup is the **read amplification**, and an LSM tree has plenty unless it fights back, in two ways. A Bloom filter for each file lets most useless reads skip the disk, and compaction keeps the number of files down. Next, we'll build the filter.

try.title: Watch Cassandra flush and read
steps: From the `labs` folder, start Cassandra with `docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml up -d --wait` (it takes about a minute). Then open a shell, a window for typing commands, inside its container: `docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml exec cassandra bash`.

sections.h: A Bloom filter: about 10 bits per key that say "definitely not here"
sections.body:
A read wants to skip every SSTable that doesn't hold its key, without reading the file. Version 1 keeps the set of every file's keys in memory. That's the trouble with the store in Bytes, pages and durability again: 200 million keys of 40 bytes take 8 GB.

Version 2 gives up exact answers. Keep an array of m bits, all 0, and one hash function: a formula that turns any key into a number that looks random but is always the same for the same key. To add a key, set the bit at `hash(key) mod m`, the remainder after dividing by m. To check a key, look at its bit. A 0 means no key that lands there was ever added, so the key is certainly absent, and the file can be skipped. A 1 means "maybe": this key was added, or another key landed on the same bit.

With 10 bits per key, about 1 bit in 10 is set, so about 1 absent key in 10 gets a wrong "maybe", a **false positive**. A false positive costs one wasted block read. A wrong "no" would hide data, and this structure never gives one.

Version 3 is the **Bloom filter**, from Burton Bloom in 1970, which uses k hash functions instead of one. Adding a key sets k bits, and a key is "maybe present" only if all k of its bits are 1. More hashes set more bits, but an absent key must now hit k set bits by chance instead of one. For n keys in m bits, the false-positive rate is about (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k. You don't need to remember it; the Try it checks it. The rate is lowest when k is about 0.69 times the bits per key. At 10 bits per key, that gives k = 7 and a rate of 0.82%. The figure shows a tiny filter giving both answers.

On the clerk's shelf, the filter is a card of squares on each booklet's cover. For each form she binds, she inks the few squares its number picks. If any square of a number is blank, that form isn't inside, and she doesn't open the booklet.

The cost is small and predictable, which is why every SSTable gets one. RocksDB's documentation gives 1% at 9.9 bits per key and 0.1% at 15.5. Cassandra's default `bloom_filter_fp_chance` is 0.01, a 1% target, and in the last Try it its filter for 1,000 keys took 1,264 bytes, about 10 bits per key. A filter is built once, when its file is written. You can't remove a key from a Bloom filter, but a file that never changes never needs to.

Bloom filters have one hard limit: they answer "is this exact key here?" and nothing else. A range question, such as "every payment of card 4242 today", can't use them. It must open every file whose keys overlap the range. So the filters cut the useless reads, but the files keep piling up. Next, we'll merge them.

sections.h: Compaction merges files, and each way of merging picks a cost
sections.body:
Without compaction, files pile up. Every flush adds one, reads check more of them, and every overwritten value and deleted key keeps taking disk space. The disk bytes per byte of live data, the data a read can still return, is the **space amplification**. The log in Bytes, pages and durability reached 100 before a merge.

Compaction works like merging sorted piles of cards: look at the top card of each pile, take the smallest, and repeat. Read several SSTables in key order at once, keep only the newest version of each key, write the result as new SSTables, then delete the inputs. The clerk does it at night with a few booklets. A tombstone can be dropped only when no older file could still hold its key. Drop it any earlier, and the old value comes back. The stepper's last frame and the lab's `compact` merge everything into one file, so they can drop every tombstone.

Real stores merge a few files at a time. How they pick the files is the main setting of an LSM tree, and it sets all three amplifications at once.

Leveled compaction is RocksDB's default. Flushed files go into level 0, where their key ranges overlap. When level 0 has 4 files, they're merged into level 1. Each level below 0 is one sorted run, with every key at most once and in order, cut into files of 64 MB by default whose key ranges don't overlap. Each level is about 10 times bigger than the one above. A read checks the level-0 files, then at most one file per level. The price is writing. A key is rewritten each time it moves down a level, and merging into a level 10 times bigger rewrites the overlapping files there too. RocksDB's wiki says leveled compaction's write amplification is often larger than 10.

Size-tiered compaction, still the default in Cassandra 5.0, waits for 4 files of similar size and merges them into one bigger file. Each byte is rewritten far fewer times. But a key can sit in many files, so reads check more of them, and a merge needs free disk space for its whole output.

Cassandra 5.0 added the Unified Compaction Strategy (UCS), which its docs recommend for new tables. It shows that the two styles are ends of one dial. One setting picks the fanout f, how many times bigger each level is than the one above. `T4`, the default, is tiered with f = 4, the old size-tiered behaviour. `L10` is leveled with f = 10, like the old leveled strategy. Leveled writes grow with (f - 1) times the number of levels, and leveled reads with the number of levels; tiered is the mirror image. For 1 TB of data and 1 GB flushes, L10 has 3 levels and T4 has 5. So leveled writes about 5 times as much (9 x 3 = 27, against 5), and tiered checks about 5 times as many files per lookup (3 x 5 = 15, against 3).

One Cassandra detail shows up in the Try it. Compaction keeps a tombstone for `gc_grace_seconds`, 10 days by default, even when it could drop it. Cassandra keeps copies of each row on several computers, called replicas, and one of them may have missed the delete. Without the tombstone, a repair, the job that brings replicas back in line, would copy the old row back from it. Cassandra's docs call a deleted row that returns this way a zombie. Next, we'll weigh the whole design against the B+tree.

Run `nodetool compact` to merge every SSTable of the table into one, then dump partition 500 from the result with `sstabledump`, which prints a file's contents. Predict: is the tombstone gone?
When you're done with this lesson, leave the shell (type `exit`) and stop Cassandra from the `labs` folder: `docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml down -v`.

sections.h: The evidence: what Facebook measured, and when each design wins
sections.body:
No design wins at everything. The RUM conjecture (Manos Athanassoulis and colleagues, 2016) says so with three costs: read, update and memory, meaning space. Put a limit on two of them, and the third has a floor it can't go below. A B+tree limits reads to 3 or 4 pages, and pays with a page write per random insert and with partly empty pages. An LSM tree makes writes sequential, and pays with reads through several files and with dead versions kept until compaction.

The best evidence comes from Facebook. It moved its main MySQL user database, UDB, from InnoDB, MySQL's B+tree engine, to MyRocks, which is MySQL on RocksDB, and finished in August 2017. The same data took 62.3% less space than in compressed InnoDB, and bytes written to flash storage fell by 75%. The processor's work fell slightly, and read latency, how long a read takes, stayed about the same. UDB ran on less than half as many computers.

The paper (Yoshinori Matsunobu, Siying Dong and Herman Lee, VLDB 2020) names where InnoDB lost. Splits left 25% to 30% of each page empty, and packing pages full again didn't last under random writes. Compression had to fit each 16 KB page into a fixed 8 KB slot, so a page that compressed to 5 KB still took 8 KB. And a one-row change rewrote a whole page, twice counting InnoDB's doublewrite buffer, which Write-ahead logging and crash recovery explains. RocksDB, tuned, kept dead data to about 10%.

That isn't a verdict that LSM trees are faster. UDB was write-heavy, and the data it used often didn't fit in memory, which is where B+trees suffer most. Short benchmarks, tests that time a store for a few minutes, flatter LSM trees, because an empty store has nothing to compact. Once compaction competes with new writes, writes per second drop, and RocksDB slows or stops writes when compaction falls behind. Range scans favour B+trees, because a scan merges every level, and Bloom filters can't help it. So test your own mix of reads and writes, for long enough that compaction starts.

**Many writes, read back by key: an LSM tree. Many reads and ranges: a B+tree.** When disk space costs real money, that counts for the LSM tree too.

Large values add one more choice. Compaction copies values along with keys, so a 4 KB reply from the bank, stored with each payment, is rewritten at every level, although only its key decides where it goes. WiscKey (Lanyue Lu and colleagues, FAST 2016) keeps only keys and a pointer in the LSM tree and appends values to a separate log. It loaded data 2.5 to 111 times faster than LevelDB, an older LSM store from Google, and served random lookups 1.6 to 14 times faster. In exchange, a lookup needs one more read for the value, a range scan turns into scattered value reads, and the value log needs its own clean-up. RocksDB ships the idea as BlobDB: with `enable_blob_files` on, values of at least `min_blob_size` bytes go to separate blob files.

And both designs lean on a log we haven't opened yet: the one beside the memtable, and the one PostgreSQL wrote 26 MB to in the first Try it.

compare.title: One random-key insert: B+tree and LSM tree

a.label: B+tree (PostgreSQL)
a.title: update in place
a.src:
1. descend the index: root and internal page (cached)
2. read the leaf: probably not cached, a random read
3. change the leaf in memory, mark it dirty
4. WAL record; a full page image if this is the
   page's first change since the checkpoint
5. later: write the whole 8 KB page back

write cost: about one page per insert
read cost:  one page per level

b.label: LSM tree (RocksDB)
b.title: write out of place
b.src:
1. append to the WAL
2. insert into the memtable (RAM)
3. later: flush 64 MB of sorted keys in one
   sequential write
4. later: compaction rewrites the key at each
   level it moves through

write cost: a few bytes now, rewritten ~10x later
read cost:  memtable + one file per level, minus
            the files the Bloom filters skip

compare.note: The B+tree pays at write time, a page for each random insert, and in return a read is one short walk down the tree. The LSM tree makes the write itself almost free and sequential, then pays later, in the background, with compaction, and at read time with several places to look. Neither is faster in general; the workload decides.

worked.title: Size the Bloom filters for a store of payment ids

steps.say: The store will hold 200 million payment ids across its SSTables. Start from the false-positive rate you want, p. The bits per key that give rate p, with the best number of hashes, follow from the formula: m/n = -ln(p) / (ln 2)^2.
steps.code:
import kotlin.math.ln

fun bitsPerKey(p: Double) = -ln(p) / (ln(2.0) * ln(2.0))

bitsPerKey(0.01)   // 9.59
bitsPerKey(0.001)  // 14.38

steps.say: Turn bits per key into memory. The filters stay in memory, so this is a real line in the budget.
Pick the number of hashes: about 0.69 times the bits per key. More hashes cost processor time on every lookup, and fewer raise the false-positive rate.
steps.code:
k = 0.69 x 9.59 = 6.6, so 7 hashes for 1%
k = 0.69 x 14.38 = 9.9, so 10 hashes for 0.1%

steps.say: Decide with the read cost. A lookup of an id that isn't stored yet, the common case when the store checks whether a payment is new, must ask every file it can't rule out. With 8 files to check, 1% filters waste 0.08 block reads per lookup instead of 8. Going to 0.1% saves 0.07 reads for 120 MB more memory. Take 1% unless misses dominate and memory is cheap.
steps.code:
expected wasted reads = files checked x p
  no filters: 8 x 1.0   = 8
  1%:         8 x 0.01  = 0.08
  0.1%:       8 x 0.001 = 0.008

lab.title: Build an LSM store: memtable, SSTables and Bloom filters
steps: Read the file format at the top of `SSTable.kt`, then `write`, `open` and `entries`, which are done. In `BloomFilter.kt`, read `hash64`, `bitIndex`, `setBit` and `getBit`.
Run the tests once from the `labs` folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All 13 fail for now.
Write `BloomFilter.add` and `mightContain`. Split `hash64(key)` into two 32-bit halves and use `bitIndex(h1, h2, i)` for i = 0 until `hashes`. The three `BloomFilterTest` tests pass.
Write `SSTable.get`: the filter first, then `blockFor`, then one read of the whole block, then a scan of its records.
Write `LsmStore.put`, `delete`, `get` and `flush`. Remember that `tables` is newest first.
Write `compact`. Run the tests until all 13 pass.
hints: `memtable[key]` returns null both for a tombstone and for a missing key. `memtable.containsKey(key)` tells them apart.

In `SSTable.get`, a block ends where the next block starts, or at `dataEnd` for the last block. Allocate a `ByteBuffer` of exactly that size and fill it with the `readFully` helper: that's the one read the test counts.
While you scan a block, stop as soon as a record's key is greater than the one you want. The records are sorted.
In `compact`, walk `tables.asReversed()` (oldest first) into one `TreeMap`, so newer versions overwrite older ones, then drop the null values before you write.

drill.title: Write the read path and compaction from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. You have a `memtable: TreeMap<String, ByteArray?>`, where null is a tombstone, and `tables: List<SSTable>`, newest first, where `SSTable.get` returns `Value`, `Tombstone` or `Missing`. Write `get(key)` and `compact()`. Then answer: why may `compact` drop tombstones here, and when may a real store not?

recap: A B+tree insert with a random key dirties a whole page and, after a checkpoint, logs a copy of that page. An LSM tree collects writes in a sorted memtable in memory and writes them out as one sequential file.
An SSTable is a file of records in key order that never changes, with a sparse index (the first key of each block) and a Bloom filter, both kept in memory.
A read checks the memtable, then the SSTables from newest to oldest, and stops at the first hit. A tombstone means "deleted" and stops the search.
A Bloom filter never says no for a key it holds. With about 10 bits per key and 7 hashes, it gives a wrong "maybe" about 1% of the time, and it can't help range questions.

Compaction merges files, keeps the newest version of each key, and drops a tombstone only when no older file can hold its key. Leveled compaction favours reads and often rewrites data more than 10 times; size-tiered favours writes; Cassandra 5.0's UCS puts both on one dial.

The limit: no design wins everywhere. Facebook's MyRocks used 62% less space and wrote 75% fewer bytes than InnoDB, but B+trees keep the edge on ranges and steady reads, and LSM writes slow down when compaction falls behind.
closing:
We started with 10,000 small fraud records that made a B+tree write 26 MB to its log. An LSM tree would have sorted them in memory and written them out once, in one long write, then paid later, in the background, with compaction.

Next time you run the Cassandra Try it, type `nodetool tablestats lsm.auths` without the `grep`. Find the Bloom filter lines: how much space the filter takes, and how many false positives it has given so far.

Next, we'll open the log that sits beside every memtable and every buffer pool. When a database says a change is saved, what has really reached the disk?

quiz.q: A store has four SSTables. You delete `card:7`: its tombstone is in the newest SSTable, and the oldest SSTable still holds `card:7 = ACTIVE`. A compaction merges only the two newest SSTables. May it drop the tombstone?
options: Yes: the tombstone has done its job once it's merged
No: the oldest SSTable still holds card:7, and without the tombstone, reads would find ACTIVE again
Yes, but only if the memtable is empty
No: tombstones are never removed from an LSM tree
quiz.why: A tombstone hides older versions of its key. A read stops at the first file that knows the key, so if the merged file had no entry for card:7, the read would fall through to the oldest file and return ACTIVE: a deleted card comes back. The first option is the tempting one, because the merge does feel like the end of the tombstone's work. Tombstones are removed once a compaction includes every older file that could hold the key, which is why the last option is wrong too.

quiz.q: A store keeps a 4 KB reply from the bank with each payment, keyed by payment id, written once and read back by id. Compaction keeps the disk busy most of the time. Which change cuts that work the most?
options: More bits per key in the Bloom filters
Switch from size-tiered to leveled compaction
Key-value separation (RocksDB's BlobDB, the WiscKey idea), so compaction moves keys and small pointers instead of 4 KB values
A bigger memtable, so each flush writes fewer files
quiz.why: Compaction rewrites everything in the files it merges, so the 4 KB values are most of its work. With the values in a separate log, each merge copies a key and a pointer of a few dozen bytes. Bloom filters save reads, not compaction work. Leveled compaction rewrites more, not less. A bigger memtable makes fewer, bigger flushes, but every value is still rewritten as it moves down the levels.

quiz.q: On an LSM store with 6 SSTables, you ask a range question: every payment of card 4242 between 09:00 and 10:00 (keys `card:4242:<time>`). How do the Bloom filters help?
options: They don't: a whole-key filter only answers "is this exact key here?", so the scan opens every file whose key range overlaps
They skip every file that doesn't contain card 4242
They return the keys in the range directly, without reading the files
They halve the number of files, like a binary search
quiz.why: A Bloom filter is built from hashes of whole keys, and hashing scrambles the order, so it can't say whether any key between two bounds is present. The scan merges every SSTable whose key range overlaps. The second option is the trap: it would need a filter of card numbers, not of whole keys. RocksDB does have such prefix filters for stores whose every query fixes the same front part of the key, but a plain whole-key filter can't do it.

quiz.q: A fraud check writes 50,000 events a second with random keys and reads back fewer than 100 a second, by exact key. Which compaction style fits, and why?
options: Leveled: it gives the fewest files per read, which matters most here
Size-tiered (RocksDB calls it universal compaction): it rewrites each byte fewer times, and reads are rare enough to pay for checking more files
Neither: an LSM tree can't handle that write rate
Leveled, because size-tiered can't use Bloom filters
quiz.why: The work is almost all writes, so write amplification is the cost to cut. Size-tiered merges files of similar size and rewrites each byte far fewer times than leveled, which RocksDB says often exceeds 10 times. The price is more files per read and more space, and with rare reads by exact key, the Bloom filters absorb most of that. Both styles use Bloom filters.

quiz.q: From B+trees: in this lesson's first Try it, 10,000 time-ordered inserts dirtied about 100 pages, and 10,000 random-UUID inserts dirtied about 4,300. Why the difference?
options: Random UUIDs are bigger, so each needs its own page
Ordered keys all go to the rightmost leaf, which fills and splits in turn, while random keys land on leaves all over the index
PostgreSQL squeezes ordered keys into less space
The random table had more rows to start with
quiz.why: A B+tree insert goes to the leaf where its key belongs. Growing keys always belong at the right end, so a few pages take all 10,000 inserts. Random keys belong anywhere, so nearly every insert touches a different one of the index's thousands of leaves. Both kinds of UUID are 16 bytes, and both tables started with a million rows.

flashcards.front: What is a memtable, and when is it flushed?
flashcards.back: A sorted map in memory that takes every write. When it reaches a size limit (64 MB by default in RocksDB), it's written out in key order as a new SSTable.

flashcards.front: What did Facebook measure when it moved its user database from InnoDB to MyRocks?
flashcards.back: 62.3% less space than compressed InnoDB, 75% fewer bytes written to flash, slightly less CPU time and about the same read latency.

flashcards.front: In what order does an LSM read check its data, and when does it stop?
flashcards.back: The memtable, then the SSTables from newest to oldest. It stops at the first one that knows the key; a tombstone means "not found".

flashcards.front: Bloom filter: which answer is always right?
flashcards.back: "No". A 0 bit proves the key was never added. "Maybe" can be a false positive.

flashcards.front: How many bits per key for a 1% Bloom filter, and how many hashes?
flashcards.back: About 10 bits per key (RocksDB: 9.9) and 0.69 x 10, so about 7 hashes.

flashcards.front: When may compaction drop a tombstone?
flashcards.back: Only when no older file left could still hold the key. Cassandra also waits for gc_grace_seconds, 10 days by default.

flashcards.front: Leveled or size-tiered compaction, in one line each?
flashcards.back: Leveled: at most one file per level per read, but data is often rewritten more than 10 times. Size-tiered: fewer rewrites, more files to read and more spare space needed.

terms.plain: A store that collects writes in a sorted map in memory, writes them out as sorted files that never change, and merges those files in the background.
The sorted map in memory that takes every write until it's flushed to disk.
Sorted string table: a file of records in key order that never changes once written, with a small index and a Bloom filter.
A marker written in place of a deleted key, saying "deleted", so older files can't bring the key back.
An array of bits and a few hash functions that answers "definitely not present" or "maybe present" for a key.
Merging SSTables into new ones, keeping the newest version of each key and dropping what it safely can.
Bytes written to disk for each byte of data stored. Page rewrites raise it in a B+tree, and compaction in an LSM tree.
How many disk reads one lookup needs. In an LSM tree it grows with the number of files to check.

explain_back.prompt: A friend asks why RocksDB, a storage library, can take tens of thousands of writes a second on one disk, while a PostgreSQL table keyed by random UUIDs struggles at a few thousand. Explain what each does on a write, and what RocksDB pays for its speed.
explain_back.answer: PostgreSQL keeps the index as a B+tree and changes it in place. Each insert with a random key belongs on a different leaf page, so it reads that leaf, changes the whole 8 KB page in memory, logs a full copy of the page if it's the first change since the last checkpoint, and later writes the page back. That's kilobytes of disk work for a few dozen bytes of data. RocksDB appends the write to its log and puts it in a sorted map in memory, the memtable. When the memtable fills, it writes it out as one sorted file, in one long sequential write. The price comes later and elsewhere. Compaction rewrites the same data several times as it merges files, often ten times or more with leveled compaction, and a read may have to look in the memtable and several files, newest first. Bloom filters keep most of those extra reads off the disk, but they can't help range questions.

deeper.body:
**Which files make up the database?** The lab trusts the file names on disk. That breaks if a crash hits in the middle of a compaction, after the new file is written but before the inputs are deleted. On restart both are there, and since the merged file has no entry for a key whose tombstone it dropped, a read falls through to an old input and the deleted value comes back. RocksDB keeps a MANIFEST, a small log of changes to the set of live files. "Add these outputs, remove these inputs" is one record, so a compaction takes effect all at once or not at all. Files that the MANIFEST doesn't list are deleted at startup.

**The memtable's own log.** The memtable is lost in a crash, so every write first goes to a write-ahead log. Once a memtable is flushed, its part of the log is no longer needed and is deleted. Write-ahead logging and crash recovery builds such a log and the recovery that replays it. Cassandra calls its log the commit log.

**Smaller filters, and fewer levels to search.** RocksDB's Ribbon filter (since version 6.15) gives the same false-positive rate in about 30% less space, for 3 to 4 times the processor time. With `level_compaction_dynamic_level_bytes`, the default since RocksDB 8.4, the level sizes are worked out from the last level, which ends up holding about 90% of the data, so space amplification stays near 1.1.

**Range scans in an LSM tree.** A scan opens a reader on the memtable and on every SSTable whose key range overlaps, and merges them in key order, as compaction does, skipping old versions and tombstones. Leveled compaction keeps that to one file per level. This is also where Cassandra's choice to sort by a hash of the key shows: ranges only work inside one partition.

**Deletes aren't free.** A common mistake is to use a Cassandra table as a to-do list: insert a row per job, delete it when it's done, and read "the oldest jobs". Every delete writes a tombstone, and a read of that list must step over all of them until compaction removes them, which waits at least `gc_grace_seconds`. Cassandra warns when one query reads 1,000 tombstones and fails it at 100,000 (`tombstone_warn_threshold` and `tombstone_failure_threshold`). Put deleted data where nobody reads again, for example one partition per hour of work, or use a log built for queues.
